Insofar as the high value which capitalism places on property and the desire to possess reinforces and perpetuates the ignorance which Buddhism tries to eliminate root and branch, Buddhism takes its stand in opposition to capitalism. As non-possession is a result of the non-self, Buddhism and capitalism are in opposition, as the latter favours possession and private property, while the former teaches detachment. Without the possession of goods, the capitalist system cannot exist, since it is based on income and investment that leads to the reproduction of these goods and the acquisition of new ones, or rather the accumulation; in order to afterwards be reinvested and to continue the cycle. It is craving which renews being and is accompanied by relish and lust, relishing this and that: in other words, craving for sensual desires, craving for being, craving for non-being. But whereon does this craving arise and flourish? Wherever there is what seems lovable and gratifying, thereon it arises and flourishes. (Samyutta Nikaya LVI, 11 as cited in Sumedho 2011, 19) For the purposes of the discussion about consumption, kama tanha is emphasised. Sumedho (2011, 19) describes it as “wanting sense pleasures through the body or the other senses and always seeking things to excite or please your senses.” But notice that desire itself is not the cause of suffering. Suffering happens because there is attachment to desire. Desire comes from ignorance (avijja), because it derives from attachment. Desire is the reason for consumption. In the current socioeconomic model, desires are encouraged and created by marketing campaigns, by programmed obsolescence, by what is in fashion, generating superfluous consumption. Thus, desires are only limited by scarcity (of the desired good or the income to buy it). According to Buddhist teaching, desires must be controlled by moderation and by the pursuit of genuine well-being. Here, consumption must be accompanied by a real purpose of supplying basic, personal, and collective needs, avoiding unnecessary consumption in tune with chanda. Consumption is seen as a means to achieve the ultimate goal of enhancing human development. For example, the consumption of food aims to nourish the consumer physically and mentally so that they can develop spiritually, not primarily for the pleasure it provides. Consequently, the consumption provided by desire that does not contribute to personal development is tanha. In other words, non-consumption can contribute to our well-being. Consumption is an essential macroeconomic variable in modern economics and capitalism. Schumacher (1973, 58) states that: “[Modern economics] considers consumption to be the sole end and purpose of all economic activity, taking the factors of production—land, labour, and capital—as the means.” Many government policies rely on consumer incentives as the driver of economic growth (Chai 2018), with the dissemination of campaigns for personal loans for the acquisition of consumer goods.
